utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are ready to continue, your Honour. Perhaps the witness might be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning. We are going to continue now. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. BAHTIJA SIVRO (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Good morning, colleagues of the Defence and good morning, Mr. Sivro. Do you feel comfortable this morning? I left you yesterday on the morning of April 19th. What happened, can you tell the court what happened on that morning? You had been within your apartment practically in confinement. What did you expect about yourself, your information about where most main Muslims were arrested, some of them even killed. What were your thoughts at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, I am ready to continue. As I said yesterday, I was woken up by explosions about 5.00 in the morning on 16th April 1993. My wife and children were already awake, looking through the window I could see in the distance shooting around the town and in the position of the village of Ahmici, some houses were already burning and the shooting continued, there was a lot of smoke and fire. Firing could be heard around town. I realised that the war in Vitez had started between the Croatian Defence Council and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: May I stop you for a moment? Now we are referring to a subsequent day, the 19th, some days after the beginning on the 16th. We already know that on the 16th a conflict had started. Let us go to 19th April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, on the 19th in the evening about 7.00 pm, I saw through the window that Muslims were being taken into custody from the surrounding buildings and so it was the turn of my building. All able-bodied Muslims were taken into detention, together with myself, I was among them. At first, we were detained in the building of the cultural centre at the time, in the basement of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: May I stop you for a moment? So if I understand, you were not arrested individually, but you were arrested within a general action, aiming at arresting all male Muslims in that area; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: In your estimation, how many Muslim men were there in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town of Vitez itself, there were about 5,000 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I was taken to the basement of the cultural centre, where I spent two days and two nights. There were 80 to 100 men there already when I arrived, and the number kept increasing. The area was too small for so many people. It was adequate for maybe 40 to 50 people. Anything over 50 made it cramped, so that in agreement with the people who were watching over us there, who made sure that we would not leave the building, we were moved to the cinema hall and the offices upstairs, so that according to my estimate, in three or four days time, the number increased to 250 to 300 people in all these three areas within the cultural centre in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there some form of registration on your arriving there, or just were you put into the basement and left there? Were there official lists of those who were taken into the basement or in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the people who were taken to the basement were first thoroughly searched to make sure that they had no firearms or any other weapons and they were all registered. Upon arrest, at least I was told to take my ID card and a blanket, so all the people who came there had their ID cards and on the basis of that they were registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you allowed during these first days to receive visits from your relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first few days no, but two or three days later, these visits were half allowed, or rather from time to time a member of the family could come and visit us, our wives or relatives, to bring some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During detention, were prisoners, some of them, or groups of them, taken out of the theatre, the movie theatre, and for what purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was detained in the cultural centre, quite a number of people were taken to dig trenches, fortifications, dugouts and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you personally taken to do such work, or what else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not do that work, but I did clean the building itself and in front of the building, it means that I was engaged to do some work unwillingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: The people who were chosen for work, trench digging, were they chosen according to lists of their names or randomly? I make an example. Did some officer, some HVO come and ask for a certain number of persons, "we need 20 people, we need 50 people", was it like that or different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Groups were selected by random, usually younger men who were capable of doing that kind of work. Fifteen to 20 people were regularly taken and were taken for digging, for a day and a night, or two days and two nights. Unfortunately some people never returned from that digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Those who returned, in which conditions did they appear physically and psychologically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were visibly tired, dirty, frightened and exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You said you remained in the basement for a couple of days. Then did you move to some other areas in the same building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said I spent two days and two nights in the basement and then I was moved to the cinema hall. Some people remained in the basement, because I said, because it was too cramped in the basement, some were taken to the cinema hall and some to the offices. I was taken to the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During this period, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: But in this period, did you have any other meeting with Croat representatives, and if so, for what reasons, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first night after my arrest, Dr Mujezinovic came to the building, Mr. Zvonimir Cilic and Boro Jozic. Jozic and Cilic and Zvono proposed a brief meeting with us who were already in detention. Dr Mujezinovic was to take a couple of people for these talks on the possibility of halting hostilities and the destruction of the town and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I understand Dr Mujezinovic was not at that time detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he came from the improvised military infirmary which was under the supervision of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So he was there as a physician, he was there occasionally as a physician; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was working there occasionally as a doctor. I do not know whether it was of his own free will or under coercion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During this meeting, what did they ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked for about two to three hours. We were requested to halt the offensive operations of the army, or rather to suggest to army members, members of the BiH army to surrender or something to that effect. To be quite frank, this was not stated explicitly in the way I have put it, but the meaning could be interpreted in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: In this perspective, can you tell us and tell the court whether you were there as Muslim representatives which were occasionally detained or explicitly as prisoners? Did they consider you and tell you you were prisoners which were being involved in that negotiation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I was a prisoner, and all the others were virtually prisoners. This was stated by the words, "you are down there, we are here, here are the telephones, call whoever you think you should call".

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you pick up the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke that evening three times by phone with a member of the command of the local battalion housed in Kruscica, he has the same surname as I, his name is Sifret Sivro. I explained to him where we were and what we were doing and I asked him that no offensive operations should be launched from that side. The other conversation I had was with my brother in Zenica, I asked him to deny the report that Dr Mujezinovic had been killed, because he was alive and my brother did that through the media of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My third call was to Colonel Ramiz Dugalic, who was then already working in the command of the III Corps. This was very late, after 2.00 am. This was already 20th April. We also explained to him our position and we also recommended that no further movements of the troops should be made and that attempts should be invested to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivro. What happened after that? Did you receive other visits by Croat officials and military people subsequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Allow me just to say what the outcome of that meeting was. About an hour or an hour and a half later, Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak arrived and again we had the same points made and we asked that the situation in Vitez should be brought under control, and so we prepared a joint proclamation that was read out on local television. Unfortunately it bore no fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who did sign that statement? Did you particularly sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not sign it, it was signed by Dr Mujezinovic and on the other side by Mr. Ivica Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go to a subsequent period of time. Did you after that receive other -- were met by Croat officials and/or military representatives, and what did they ask you, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, there were no official contacts. Our only communication was with the local people, that is our guards. But to answer your previous question, the situation did not calm down, nor were any of the prisoners released. Visits were not prohibited; that is our closest relatives could visit us for a brief period and bring some food. They could not stay for more than five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did the number of prisoners in the cinema significantly increase or diminish during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that period, that is we are talking about April 20th, more prisoners were coming in and as I said, the figure increased to 250 to 300 people in the building in which I was put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How did it happen that you leave the building and in which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just add that in the period before leaving this building, the International Red Cross registered all the prisoners and already at the end of April, a senior military delegation of the HVO and the BiH army, both chiefs of staff, Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic, who was the commander of the HVO command, they visited us and told us orally that agreement had been reached for all of us to be released home. However, this did not happen. Some people were released, but the rest of the people stayed where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What about you at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 29th April, a considerable number of the detainees were released home, and on 4th May, very early in the morning, a few from the group that were still detained in the cinema hall were transferred to a chess club in another part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many of you were on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion, there were 12 men, then another man was brought in an hour or two after us, which makes a total of 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of some of your fellows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember. For example, engineer Suad Salkic, Cazim Ahmic, engineer Alija Basic, Professor Enes Surkovic, Fuad Kaknjo, Subasic, the late Causevic Serif, Dervis Subasic, Cazim Sahman and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you transferred to the chess club in secrecy? Did you get at that time the impression that they were hiding you, did you imagine that you were about to receive any particular treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we believed, our transfer was carried out in strict secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What did the members of this group have in common? You mentioned engineers, doctors; can you explain to the court what link possibly these people -- these 12 and later on 13 people, were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these people were Muslims, the majority were prominent figures in the economy, in business. In a word, they were prominent figures in the life of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were some of them members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some were members of the SDA, I remember well that Mr. Kadir Didic, Fuad Kaknjo, I am not sure about the others, whether they belonged to the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the ICRC aware of your situation, of the place where you were being taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The International Red Cross did not know that we had been transferred from the cinema to the chess club.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were you taken then from the chess club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in the chess club for one night and one day, a day and a half actually, and then we were summarily and very expeditiously evacuated to Kaonik, a locality close to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Had you already visited that place, that camp, or did you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew the locality, but it was -- as it was a military facility of the former Yugoslav People's Army, access was not allowed for civilians, but I was familiar with it, I knew where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where did the HVO detain you in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 13 of us were detained in a building that used to be a military warehouse which I assume was rapidly adapted into a military prison. Cells were built from building material, even concrete elements with doors being placed in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Which were the general aspect of the cell you were put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 13 of us were put up in a cell which in my estimate was adequate for four people on the outside, so there were 13 of us in this same room at the same time for two or three days we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How was the situation as to food and hygiene and general protection of your physical health?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in the cell all the time, the hygiene was below the minimum, the food was barely adequate for survival. Let me refer to a detail; as there were many of us in this cell, of course, we were all very tense and we often needed to use the toilet. In order to go there, one had to knock on the door, the guard would open the door and let one to two of us out. As I said, this happened frequently, we needed it frequently, so we were given a metal box of five litres, so that we could use it to urinate in the cell itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: On your first entering the cell, do you remember having found something unusual, some unusual object, and what did you do, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Since we were in the cell for the first time, we wanted to put it in order a little, and to clean it, if possible, to make it hygienic, so we lifted these mattresses and beneath one of them we found a big knife, and we immediately reported it to the guard who was in front of the door and told him that we had found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened? How did the guard react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guard asked us exactly where we had found it and then the commander of the guards joined him and he told us all off for how come there was a knife there. This was a brief incident and after that life continued, if one may call it, normally. This case was never referred to again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you during your stay in Kaonik interrogated, and how many times, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was interrogated. The first interrogation was outside of the building where I was kept prisoner. This was in the town of Busovaca on the premises of the accounting services, the SDK as it was called in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What did they ask you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated with respect to the Vitez trade company, which at that time traded in the explosives; who was in this company, what was the goal of this company and who works for this company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you asked to sign a statement, or to write a statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the first interrogation took place in the town of Busovaca. The second interrogation consisted of writing down of a statement. I wrote it down in the hallway in the prison, in the presence of a guard, and I wrote down my short curriculum vitae and my actions up until the time when I was imprisoned, the contacts that I had et cetera and I signed that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who actually asked you to write down your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the first interrogation took place in the town of Busovaca; there were three interrogators, one of these interrogators came to the detention and asked me to write this statement and to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During your stay at Kaonik, were you physically mistreated during interrogation or after interrogation, and in which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not physically mistreated throughout my stay in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were some of your fellow prisoners mistreated or beaten? Is that to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I think that Mr. Fuad Kaknjo was physically mistreated the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Why do you think so? Have you seen him and in which conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally saw him because as I said, we were all in a single cell, the 13 of us. These people who were taken out to be interrogated would not be brought back to the same cell, they would be taken to another cell, so I too was taken from cell number 6 to cell number 5, 16 to 5, and when Fuad Kaknjo came into number 5 I saw that he had visible bruises and he had traces of beatings on his legs and his shoulders and cheeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During your stay in Kaonik, were you visited by ECMM or ICRC officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two visits. The first visit was by the International Red Cross and they were checking on us, since we had already been registered in Vitez. Now they re-registered us in Kaonik. Immediately following this visit, the ECMM mission representatives also came to visit. Both visits were short ones and there were no special talks that were conducted at that time. I remember that the Red Cross brought us some cigarettes and they re-registered us. The UN monitors also talked to us briefly, they were escorted by the prison official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who did escort them on that particular occasion? You said prison officials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely who it was, because I was in a cell, they entered the cell. It is possible that Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski was also with them, but I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Had you already seen him before, Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know Mr. Aleksovski before my detention, but I had an opportunity to meet him and talk to him personally in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: We will go to this later on, but will you give us some more details as to the meeting with the European Community Monitoring Mission? How many of them were at that meeting? How were they dressing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there were two monitors, they were dressed in the standard white outfits, which was the regulation outfit for the European Monitors at that time. I think it was the chief of the mission for Bosnia-Herzegovina, I do not know what his name was, but I know that he was a high ranking official among the EU monitors. He asked us the usual things, how we were, how we were treated. We could not really tell him much, so we moved on to some more serene topics, like our liberation and the circumstances under which we would be set free and that indeed happened shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, just a while ago, that you met the camp commander during your stay at Kaonik. Can you state the name of the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp commander or the camp director or warden was Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you see him in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see him to my left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: In which circumstances did you meet him and how many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, we met twice in the office. My family asked about me, specifically my brother, so a member of the HVO, I think at that time he was the HVO police commander, he passed on the message and he came to see how I was and brought some cigarettes, and so this was the reason why I was in the office at the warden's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where was the office in relation to your cell? Was it in the same building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The office was in the same building not far from the cell in which I was detained at that time, maybe five or six metres away from my cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How was Mr. Aleksovski dressing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he had the so-called camouflage uniform, and that that is what he was wearing. They were all wearing that and in final analysis, it was the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did this first encounter last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski tell something to you? Did you have some conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that his mother-in-law and his wife were in Zenica and he was concerned about their fate. At that time, Zenica was under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you tell the court now about the second occasion which you met Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second meeting came shortly after the first one, maybe two or three days later. Again a guard came to my cell and took me to the warden's office, and again my brother had intervened through another friend, who came there and asked to see me, which the warden allowed, and then again we chatted a little bit and we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did the second meeting last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: In which circumstances were you then -- could you leave Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not leave the cell, I could not even leave the cell, let alone the building where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I was asking you when and how did it happen that you were exchanged or anyway you came back to your -- to a free state, personal state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left the Kaonik prison on 14th May, the whole group with the addition of two persons who were detained in another cell in another building, we were all taken back to the cinema building in Vitez, we spent two days and two nights there and on 16th May 1993, in a regular exchange which was conducted in the presence of the EC monitors and the Red Cross and other relevant persons,

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Those with whom you had been exchanged, were they military or civilians? I mean the Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. They were dressed as civilians, just as we all were civilians. Some of the Croats did not even want to leave the territory controlled by the BiH army, that is they remained in their homes, they went back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you ever return to your apartment, your house in Vitez, after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife has two or three times. I had a single opportunity, just a couple of minutes, just to take a couple of personal belongings for myself and my family. That was my only stay in my apartment in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivro. I am finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor and Mr. Sivro. I think it is now time for a break before the Defence starts the cross-examination, so we shall resume at 11.05. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just before your Honours do that, can we seek a redaction? I will just hand this up on a note from the transcript. Perhaps it could be shown to Mr. Mikulicic first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Are you agreeable, Mr. Mikulicic? Fine, then we are going to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the witness is now at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning everybody. My name is Goran Mikulicic and I represent Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski. Good morning, Mr. Sivro. I have a few questions for you, so will you please answer them to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sivro, in your statement yesterday and today, you said that in the events that you related you had contacts with the prominent persons in the political and economic life in the community where you lived, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, when the region became destabilised, did you continue to maintain these contacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you took part in many meetings in which the situation was discussed and efforts were made to find a solution to the situation, and I here mean the conflict between the two communities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, in these meetings, did you ever see present the accused, Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you said that you first saw him when you came to Kaonik for the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you hear at any time when present at the above mentioned meetings that Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski had any role that he played in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sivro, could you tell us in more detail something that you talked about, which was the interrogation by the persons when you were taken from the Kaonik facility to the town. Who was interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated by three persons. I think one person's name was Vlado Jurisic, I knew him from before the conflict and in some way, I worked with him, because he was an inspector for anti-explosives activities. At that time, I was the director of engineering and development, so I took part in his inspections of both the facilities and technology that was present in the Vitezit company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the main product of the Vitezit company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, Vitezit produced explosives for the civilian purposes, which means for mining and construction industries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As you said, Mr. Vlado Jurisic was an inspector and he was in public service. What was it called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the centre of the public security and it was also centre of security services in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know within which ministry, in other words what ministry was in charge of this sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Republican Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we could say that this was a police service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, and correct me if I am wrong, that at that time, you were also interrogated with respect to the explosives and the production of the Vitezit company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact about the traffic with explosives in this company, Vitezit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you experience this interrogation? Was this like a police interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could not be described as purely a police interrogation. I could not figure out during this interrogation, in fact I did not understand these questions, why I was being connected to the Vitez trade company when I was not part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, the questions asked of you were in regard of the explosives trade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to your stay in Kaonik. You said that you had two visits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your brother came, if I remember correctly, escorted by an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is correct then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother -- Busovaca was already under HVO control, and my brother lived and still lives in Zenica. He talked on the phone with some friends in Busovaca, because my brother worked for 15 years or more in Vatro Stelna company in Busovaca. He also had an important position there, he was an engineer, specialising in metals, so he wanted one of our acquaintances to come and visit me and see what conditions there were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who gave your brother a permit to come and visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I said that -- I think that Nikica Petrovic was his name. At that time he was a commander, I think, of the civilian police and then he became the commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I remember correctly, you said that Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski whom you saw there that time in Kaonik wore camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he wore a camouflage military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that on 16th May 1993, you were exchanged, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what role in this exchange played the accused Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had played no role in this exchange, he was not present there and it is possible that he did not know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank you very much, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivro, for your testimony. It is finished now, we have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Meddegoda will take the next witness, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution intends to call Hamdo Dautovic as its next witness. HAMDO DAUTOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I bid you welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you state your full name please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hamdo Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10th June 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Maline near Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, Mr. Dautovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim, Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Prior to April 1993, you were the owner of a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. You were owning the coffee bar even in the month of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember 18th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Why do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18th May 1993 I was arrested, I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you tell this court where you were arrested on 18th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Guca Gora near the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How far is Guca Gora from your restaurant, from your coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three kilometres, I do not know exactly. Maybe even more, I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Why did you go to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To buy cigarettes for the coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you go to Guca Gora that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my private car, of Golf make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you go alone, when you went to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mujo Beganovic came with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you buy the cigarettes in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did buy cigarettes in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Having bought the cigarettes, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I put the cigarettes in the car, and me and my friend went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you were returning home, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the way back, Ivica Bobas stopped me, who told me -- he cursed my balija mother and told me to get out of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who was Ivica Bobas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Bobas was a guy who lived close to me. He often came and patronised my coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On that occasion when he stopped your car, was he alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was he dressed in any particular uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had camouflage uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did that uniform signify to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant that he was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said Mujo Beganovic was also with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was he also stopped together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were together in the same car, I drove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you were stopped by Ivica Bobas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three other soldiers came, three other men. They told Mujo that he was free to go and Ivica Bobas ordered me to pull everything out of my pockets and put it on the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What were the three other soldiers attired in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, camouflage suits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So in all at that time there were four including Ivica Bobas, at the time after you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were any of them armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did they carry with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Bobas had an automatic rifle Kalasnjikov, two others had automatic rifles and the last one had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that Mujo Beganovic was ordered to go, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened to you at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bad things happened with me. I was taken to the police station which used to be the old Yugoslav militia station, and I waited in front, Ivica Bobas and another soldier with the rifle kept me there, I do not know how long it took, but it seemed very long to me, maybe half an hour or an hour, I do not know how long it took. But they did not take me into the room. Then the other two came, they took me into a car, a Ritmo make, and I was in this car and I knew that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you -- from the point you were arrested, how were you brought to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On foot, we just crossed the soccer field from the arrest to the police station, so it was on foot, I was between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened to the cigarettes that you had bought in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cigarettes that I bought in Guca Gora remained in the car and the car was driven away before my very eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that at the police station in Guca Gora, you were put into another car, a Fiat Ritmo car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After being put into the police station, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the police station, I waited and nothing happened. Those two soldiers guarded me, Ivica Bobas and another one. The other two went into the police station, I do not know why, probably to ask some things or to tell them about me. Then they took me into the Ritmo car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Sorry. After being put into the Ritmo car, what happened to you? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I was placed between the two soldiers in the back seat and they started driving towards Radojcici, towards Nova Bila, down the road. I had to bend my head so I could not see where we were going. I had to keep my head between my knees. Some of them hit me with the knife handle in the neck area and the other one with a rifle butt over my back. This was in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said the car was driven through Radojcici in the direction of Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We passed by Radojcici, outside Radojcici, towards Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did anything happen before you came to Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a bend to the right in the road, since I already saw that there would be no life for me I tried to jump out of the car. I hit the soldier next to me, it was not Bobas Ivica, but somebody else I did not know. The door was opened, we fell out. The car swerved from the road but Ivica Bobas ran up to me, he was very close to me and he ordered me to open my mouth, he pushed the barrel into my mouth and then they beat me as much as they wanted until I lost consciousness. All the time the barrel was in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Approximately for how long were you kept there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed to me to be an eternity and I did not have a watch, but I think it was about one hour. I do not know exactly, but it seemed a very long time, because I was beaten all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, another car, an Opel Rekord came, another vehicle and there was not enough room inside because another driver had come, so they put me in the boot of the car, in the luggage compartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thereafter, they drove along in that car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was driven in the Rekord, shut up in the trunk. There was a lot of dust. I do not know where they were taking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On the way was the car stopped at any point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The car was stopped, in front of a building. There was light. The lights were on. I heard a voice, "here we have a balija extremist for you", somebody said and somebody else said, "he is not for us, that is Hamdo. Take him away".

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You were in the boot of the car. How did you know that there were lights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew because they opened the boot and I saw the light. That is when I saw the light, from the boot of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thereafter, did the car proceed further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We continued the ride.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For about how long did the journey continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was in the boot and I was expecting to be killed. I was trying to hear what they were talking about in the car and I heard them saying that they would open the boot as if to let me go, and that they would kill me then as if I had tried to escape, so I got even more frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did the car finally come to a halt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The car stopped somewhere in the woods. The boot was opened and I was called out by an unknown voice, there were now five of them in the car, not four, "you have a child, you are a good man, you are not a bad man. We will let you go. Be careful, you must go home". I knew what was in wait for me, and I pretended to be even more badly hurt than I really was, so that I could not get up. We saw the lights of another car coming from the other direction, I do not know which make it was, and when that car reached this car that I was in, I heard a voice saying, "what is that?"; he said, "we have a balija extremist that we need to get rid of", and then I realised everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You did not leave the car when you were asked to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not get out because I know what they wanted to do. I was badly beaten, but I pretended to be even worse so that I could not get out, because I knew that a bullet was waiting for me if I did get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did your captors do to you thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, the man who came up said, "do not kill him, you should get everything he knows out of him. There is always time to kill him". When he said that, he must have been some kind of a commander, somebody that they listened to, so the boot was shut again, and then they continued the journey. I did not know where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did the car come to a halt thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, yes, the car stopped in front of a building which I did not know at the time. Afterwards I realised where I was, it was Kaonik, in front of the prison, the camp, the hangar, whatever you like to call it. I learnt everything afterwards. At the time I did not know anything. I was dragged out of the boot of the car, all beaten up. I was dragged out and I heard this man who did not have a rifle, he only had a pistol, and he said, "we are going to prepare a farewell party for you". Again I was terrified, because I thought he meant a bullet, he wanted to kill me. Fortunately they did not kill me, they beat me. They put me in the middle among four of them, like a movie, and they beat me. I was in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember what time of the day it was when you came to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was night-time. I do not know, but it was dark, because when I left my home to go to Guca Gora, it was the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Then at Kaonik, you were put into a cell in the Kaonik camp, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After they had beaten me up very badly, somebody helped me to get to the cell, there was a long corridor. For me it was very long because I could not walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you realise in which cell you had been detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a few days, I learnt that I was in cell number 3, it was cell number 3, but at first I did not know which cell it was, because they did not ask me where I was going, they just shoved me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When did you find out that it was cell number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Dragan Micic was on duty. They called him Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Dragan Micic was also a guard at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was one of the guards. He gave me water several times, he also gave me a couple of cigarettes, or at least I think it was him, because it was passed through the keyhole and I know that he did not beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you give us a description of cell number 3 in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cell number 3 in which I was detained could be described as being 2.5 by 3 or 2.75 by 3.20, something like that, roughly that was the area of the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there any windows in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a window, but facing the corridor inside. There was no window facing out. It was not a window really, but it had rails on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said there were no windows facing the outside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: This one window with bars, where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was above the door, facing the corridor, facing the inside of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there any electric lights inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no electric light in the cell, but there was an electric bulb outside in the corridor, so that the light came through the bars, through the opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What were the other facilities you had inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a blanket, a small pillow. There was a wooden bench, maybe it was 80 centimetres in concrete and then on top of it there was a wooden plank. I cannot tell you exactly. It was intended for sleeping. There was a tin can which was a toilet, the toilet for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You had to use this tin can as your toilet, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I used it. Only when Dragan Micic was on duty, he would let me spill it out and fill a plastic bottle with water. He gave me this bottle so I had some water, because I did not dare have any contact with any other guards. Every time they opened the cell, they beat me, so I preferred them not to open it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: During your period of detention, were you taken out of the cell at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken out of the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On how many occasions were you taken out of the cell, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I was taken out twice when Darko Kraljevic, Mirko Selak and Brane came, I think his surname is Jukic, he is now living in Travnik. On that occasion I was badly beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were you beaten on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken into a room with no chairs, no table. I do not know what it was, it was in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How far was it from your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not really tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was it in the same building as your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On that occasion, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion, I was interrogated by Darko Kraljevic, who asked me how many Mujahedin there were, what they were supplied with, how many arms the BiH army had and all the other things they had, whether I had a rifle, how many women I had killed, how many women I had raped, how many children I had killed, how many houses I had torched. Since I was beaten badly, I would say whatever they wanted to hear, but they beat me very much. There were another six boys in uniform. I assumed that they were the bodyguards of the three, that was my conclusion anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In what position were you when you were interrogated by these three people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In every possible position. I was standing for as long as I could stand while they beat me, then I sat down when they beat me. At the end, Brane sat on my back and beat me. I was lying down on my stomach. There was a microphone of some sort, something like a microphone in front of my mouth, and then they went on beating me and I was told to repeat whatever they said, so that I did, I repeated what they told me. This was accompanied by blows, because he was sitting on my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were interrogated on this occasion by Darko Kraljevic, Mirko Selak and Brane Jukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Mirko Selak, because he is a native of Guca Gora and that is where I completed elementary school, so that I knew him well. He did not beat me, but these other six did who were in uniform, Darko Kraljevic beat me, but Brane beat me most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you know Darko Kraljevic from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, I knew him, but only by sight. I was not in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And Brane Jukic? Did you know him also from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know Brane Jukic at all, I just -- his face seemed familiar, but I did not know him, I did not know where he came from or who or what he was. But Darko Kraljevic, I saw him in my cafe bar and in others that I used to frequent, so that Darko was familiar to me by sight, but Brane was neither known or unknown. I may have seen his face a couple of times, but I did not know him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What particular dress were they attired in at the time they interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic, Mirko Selak and Brane were in civilian clothes. I cannot remember what exactly they were wearing, but they were not in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And the other six?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other six were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the camouflage uniform, military uniform, the multi-coloured uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That uniform, did it signify anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did indicate that they were HVO soldiers, and they could be their bodyguards, two for each one of the three of them, that was my opinion as soon as I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So that was one occasion on which you were taken out of the cell. What was the second occasion on which you were taken out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the other occasion was when I was badly beaten up. I had blood in my faeces and my urine. I was afraid I would die, I did not expect to live through it. Then I complained to Dragan Micic, whom I did not know from before, but he proved to be a kind man in that camp, and then he told me that I should address myself to the warden and ask him to see a doctor, and in two days time, that happened. The warden, the director, took me to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who was the warden of the camp who took you to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you give a description of the physical appearance of Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was bald with a round face, between 35 and 40, 45 years of age, not more than that, somewhere in that range, medium height.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you recognise him if you see him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you say to this court whether he is present here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he is over there, up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the accused took you to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He drove me to the doctor in his own car, but without the lights on. I sat in the back. He was alone in the car with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What time of the day was it when he drove you to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was night-time or evening, I do not know what time it was. I know it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken to see the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got into the car and sat down, he closed the door and when he sat in the driver's seat, he said, "do not try anything because you will not succeed", and I was beaten up and incapacitated, so I did not even have any intention to try anything. I needed a doctor because I thought I would not pull out. He drove the car, I tried to ask something, but I did not get any answers, until we reached the hospital, or rather the health centre. The car stopped in front of the health centre, he told me to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you get out of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I came out of the car, I felt very weak, because I was so badly beaten, much more than is normal, and I crawled on all fours, I saw two nurses who wanted to help me, but he did not let them. The director said, "he is strong, he is able-bodied, he can walk alone", so I entered the corridor and I sat on a wooden bench in the waiting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did the accused do at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He entered the doctor's office, it was a lady doctor that time. I do not know what he did over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long was he inside the doctor's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten or fifteen minutes, not long. I was outside in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did the accused come out of the doctor's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called me in, inside the office. Together with the lady doctor was the director in the doctor's surgery. She asked me what was wrong with me, I said I was very sick, because I knew I did not dare tell her I had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said together with the lady doctor there was the director; who was this director you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko, the prison warden, the one who brought me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You are referring to the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you went into the doctor's office, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the examination room, the lady doctor asked me what was wrong with me, and I sort of tried to find the warden's eyes to see what I should say and he said that I had a cold, that I needed an injection, nothing else was wrong with me. I said to the doctor that I had blood in my stool and my urine. She told me to strip to the waist, and I did and I was completely black and blue. The doctor then told the warden, "this is animal behaviour". She took the stethoscope and she checked me out. She said, "you need treatment, treatment is needed for the patient, for Dautovic", that was me. Zlatko responded, "we have" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was Zlatko's response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko's response was that I could not stay in the hospital, that they had a separate room in the prison for medical -- I do not know how he called it, how he called that room where they kept the sick, I do not know if he called it the infirmary or what, but he said he had a room where the sick were being treated in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you treated at the health centre by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received an injection, I do not know what it was, that is all I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Then what happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I again got into the warden's car, and the warden turned on the ignition and started. It was night and he went towards the camp. Then through tears I requested, "please cut down on the beating and cut down on my portions of food, because I cannot eat from all the beating", and then he said, "nobody will beat you any more". He promised me that nobody would beat me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you came back to the camp, were you treated at the medical facility in the camp as promised by the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was returned to the same cell, same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did the beatings stop in accordance with your pleadings to the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From then on, I was beaten more. I received more beatings, because the cell was open and the three came in and beat me, they said, "he is the one who complained about the beating". Then I regretted for having complained to the warden, because I was receiving more beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I go back to my earlier question. When you came back to the camp, were you treated at the medical facility as promised by the accused. Did you receive any medication at all in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received an injection in the infirmary, but this was where I was examined by the doctor, and for me, that infirmary in the prison was really the cell where I was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What were the other occasions on which you were taken out of the cell during the period of your detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an occasion when four of us were brought out of the cell, when Zlatko and a group of his guards, his soldiers, I do not know who they were, they created a sort of little play with us. It was me, Muhamed from Syria, Ivica Marus from the Dorci area and some Zlajo, I do not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you tell this Trial Chamber what this play was all about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called it a monodrama, a play. We had to lie down on our backs and create a cross. I will describe it, also I will try to show it. My legs were here and my head was there and then Kun's legs were next to mine, Ivica's legs were here and head there and Zlajo's head was here and legs here (indicates). Then we were told to sing and to sing it very loud so it could be heard well. I was ordered to say, "for King and country". Muhamed Kun was to say, "Comrade Tito, we give you an oath". For Ivica it was to be "Allah Akbah". It was all to be said in unison. Since I was beaten up badly and did not have any voice left, I was beaten a lot because I was not able to say, "for King and country". They thought that I would not say these things. I was going to say anything just not to be beaten, but I could not, so I was beaten a lot. There was a lot of laughter on that occasion and Zlatko was among them. They talked, they chatted, they beat us, we were there at their mercy lying down and this went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Dautovic, I would want you to go back to this incident. I know the pain of mind and the pain of body that was inflicted on you, but I want to take you back to this particular incident. You said you were asked to lie down with three others on the floor, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on our backs and the head pointing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Then you described how your feet were touching each other together, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, our feet touched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You were lying in the form of a cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So when you were lying in this position, it is when you were lying in this position you had to say the words that you were ordered to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but very loud, altogether in unison. Not individually, but altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened if you did not say it loud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beatings, blows. I received the most beating at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who beat you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unknown persons, persons who were there unknown to me. Zlatko did not beat me but he watched, he was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The accused was also present on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was present to this monodrama or play.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: These persons who beat you on this occasion, were they officials of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. There were two or three in jeans and the rest of them were in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Obviously that uniform signified the HVO to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not ascribe it any other meaning but that they were the HVO, because they could not have been anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there other occasions on which you were taken out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought out when the International Red Cross came to take down our information, that was brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About how long after you were taken into detention did the International Red Cross come over to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not count the days very much, I was always beaten up and sick, so I could barely say when it was day and when it was night. I only knew that it was night because I was beaten less at night. I guess they were sleeping. When they would beat me -- when they would cease to beat me, I would assume it was night. So I do not know, about 18 to 20 days may have passed from the time I was detained until the Red Cross arrived, but I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did the International Red Cross do with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They gave me, and I have this with me from the International Red Cross, I have an ID card with a name and last name, date of birth, residence, and that meant something to me. I was glad because Dragan Micic said, "you should feel lucky the International Red Cross registered you, because then you would not be killed", so I was glad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So in short you were registered by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Going back to the conditions -- Mr. Dautovic, if I can take you back to the conditions at the camp, did you have adequate drinking water in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had even too much drinking water. Whenever Dragan Micic was on duty, he would give me water, but I could not drink much of it, because I think I did not eat more than two or three meals throughout this period, because I was always beaten up. I always had water in this plastic bottle which contained one or two litres. I occasionally used it to take a drink of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So it was only when Dragan Micic was there that you got drinking water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I could empty the tin can that I used to relieve myself and to get the fresh water. I did not want contact with others, because I was beaten up constantly, there were times when I would shiver with fear when somebody would say -- ask for keys to open the door, and sometimes he said that he did not have the keys, so several times he protected me from being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have water to wash yourself during the period of your detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not even wash my hands throughout my period of detention. I did not wash anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have toilet facilities in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a can. To me that was the toilet facility for me, it was this tin can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As you said before, that was the can which you emptied when Dragan was on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In the camp, did you have facilities for religious observances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in my thoughts and in my wishes, but without success. I did not even dare ask about it, I probably would have had my throat slit or something, so in my thoughts and inside, I did have that, but not outwardly, I did not dare ask for any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: During the period of detention, were you deployed on work outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I wanted to go, because Dragan Micic told me that those who went out to dig dugouts and trenches, that they are not beaten, they would come back and spend the night and go out again, so I wanted to do that, but I was not in the shape to dig because I was considered a balija extremist, a Mujahedin. I was called "mungus" in the camp. I even learned some songs in the camp which I had to sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What were the songs you had to sing in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "From here to Fruska Gora, they are all Draza's guards and Nikola Pavelic's patrols." This I had to learn by heart and this happened several times a day, 50, 20, 10 times, 100 times, whichever, whatever people wanted, and other people sang too. If there were two knocks it was not me, so I had to listen whether he would knock two or three times to see who was going to have to sing, and so I could not go to sleep, because if they knocked and I was asleep and did not hear the knocking then I would be beaten, so I had to be very alert to hear when they would knock. Several times when the door opened, they would say, "see how the balija sings" and they would knock three times, they would say, "Fruska Gora", and that was my song, I had to sing that. This was the house order, you had to do whatever they tell you to do and I did whatever I could. Not everything that I was ordered to do, I said and I did everything so that I would be beaten less. But I would always get beaten. However, thank to God I survived. They I think did not expect me to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could you ask the witness what he meant by the word "mungus"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Dautovic, you said you were called in the camp, you were called a balija extremist and you were also called a mungus. Could you tell this court what is meant by the term "mungus"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was an abbreviation for Mujahedin, mungus. Balija extremist means Muslim extremist, which I was neither, because I too had problems with Mujahedin, because they do not drink alcohol, so I never had any contact with these people. Because of my business, I never had any dealings with them, I did not have an opportunity to communicate with them, because I was ignored by them, but for Zlatko I was a mungus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You told this court that you had to sing upon three knocks and two knocks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not twice or three times, but exactly three times. If they would knock twice and I would sing, then I would be beaten, because it was not my cue to sing. For me it was not two or three times, it was exactly three knocks for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So it would be three knocks for you to sing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who gave you such instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received these instructions when I first came to the camp, I cannot remember exactly whether it was the warden or someone else, I do not know, that I do not know who gave them, because at that time, I was scared and I was not sure whether I would be alive or I would die, so I do not know who gave them to me, but I knew that I had to stick to them, because on several occasions, I was beaten because of the singing. They had a knife in their hand and they said, "balija, listen good to this song. If you memorise it, you will be fine; if not, you will have your throat slit". So I had to remember it, I had to memorise it, and I do not think I will ever forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Apart from Dragan Micic, do you remember any other guards who were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember anybody by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Medugorac, who beat me the most and who told me that I would not come out alive from them. He beat me the most and for me it was like a death sentence when he would be there, because there would always be beatings there, and if anybody wanted to beat any of the balijas, I was the one. They would say, "we had some drinks but we did not have any snacks, so we need some snacks, what do we do?". Then I would be beaten, that would be the snacks. The worst moments would be as the cell was being unlocked and the expectation to be beaten, then it was the beatings themselves, 10, 20 blows, kicks. I became immune to the beatings in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
