utterances.text: The political leadership of the HDZ and, of course, with the armed units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said there were incidents of harassment and mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim intellectuals were taken into custody by the HVO for some sort of interrogations. The Muslim coffee shops, shops and property were blown up. Just before the outbreak of the conflict, there was a murder. Mirsad Delija was murdered. All this heightened tension, caused fear among the Muslim population living in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall when Mirsad Delija was killed? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly, but I think it was on 21st January. I think it was 21st January.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Of which year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993, just before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, when the situation in Busovaca was getting out of hand, what steps did you take with regard to the safety and security of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 15th January, I simply moved my family from Busovaca to stay with another family that is related to us, in the interests of their safety, because there were increasingly frequent explosions and blowing up of establishments.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you were mobilised into the TO, were you in possession of a firearm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at first, however later --

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When were you given a firearm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first time I went to the front in Visoko, I had a pistol of 7.62 calibre, issued by the Territorial Defence, and I had a licence to carry it.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was that pistol at any point in time confiscated from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was confiscated? If you do not, it is all right. If you remember approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date. I have a certificate somewhere, which I have shown to the Tribunal, and on that certificate is the exact date, but I cannot remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was it before the killing of Mirsad Delija, or was it after? The confiscation of your weapon was before the killing of Mirsad Delija or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember who confiscated your pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, members of the regional HVO police, a man called Dusko Prusac and Darko Marusic.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said to this Chamber a while ago that Mirsad Delija was killed on 21st January 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you attend his funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 22nd, I think, or the 23rd, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember the day after Mirsad Delija's funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was that the day on which you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 24th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were you arrested on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested at the railway station opposite the bus station in Busovaca, in front of the UNPROFOR base. I think that the UNPROFOR policemen were accommodated in that base at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Together with you, was anybody else also arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my father.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sead Hajdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who arrested you on 24th January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know that they were members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they had the insignia. I do not remember which side, on their sleeves they had the HVO insignia. I knew some of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of those persons who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljo Sakic and the other one's name was also Zeljo, but I do not know his surname. He was nicknamed "Bubreg", or "Kidney".

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What time of the day was it that you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At 6.15 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you were arrested, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was arrested, we were taken to the bus station where they had a military police outpost and since we knew the commander of that police, his name was Vlado Cosic, we insisted that he receive us to tell us why we were being arrested. However, they did not allow this and after that, they locked us up in the anteroom to the toilet at the same bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You and your father Sead were both taken together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you were taken to this anteroom in the bus station, did you see others whom you knew who had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were already four or five men there who were brought there before us, and in the meantime, Mirsad Dizdarevic was brought there too, while we were asking to be received by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said when you went there there were about four or five others. Did you know any of them who were already there, who were already arrested and kept in the bus station room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall any names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was Remsija Kutic and Mirsad Dizdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you wanted to see Vlado Cosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Why did you want to see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We wanted an explanation as to why we were arrested, the reasons for it, because it was not clear to us why we were being detained.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to see Vlado Cosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: At that time, were you given the reasons for your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but before the arrest, this Zeljo, whose nickname was Bubreg, he first saw us at the bus station and when he realised who -- recognised myself and my father, he told my father and me to go home, because there was some kind of a conflict near Kacuni and not to leave the house. However, Zeljo Sakic, who was also there, said we should be detained at their police station there at the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So for how long were you detained at the bus station, Mr. Hajdarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about four hours, so that around 10.00 we were transferred to the Kaonik camp, which was the former barracks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I will come to that. Before you were transferred, you said you were kept there for about four hours. About how many others were there at the time before you were transported, about how many people altogether were arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to ten people.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So after about four hours at this bus station room, you were transported to Kaonik, you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you transported by Kaonik? By what means of transport were you taken to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By bus.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where in Kaonik were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the hangars. There was a hangar which had already been reconstructed as a prison, with cells. At the entrance to Kaonik, which was the former barracks, this is where the former JNA was, that is where they took us and then they put us in one of the hangars where I assumed they used to keep some equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Had you been to this Kaonik barracks before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were taken to Kaonik and the bus took you to Kaonik, and how were you taken to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered the compound of this former barracks, the bus came to a stop in front of the first building, the first structure that is there in this compound. Then we were taken out of the bus and, under escort, taken to this prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please show to this court where you had alighted at Kaonik and which building you were taken to in Kaonik? Your Honours, may I be permitted to show this map of Kaonik, which I move to mark as Exhibit P8. Mr. Hajdarevic, could you please show us the place at which you and the others had to alight when you were brought to Kaonik that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evening when we were brought in, the bus entered the compound and we had to alight the bus at this place and then we went down this road to this hangar here.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please mark the building at the place at which you alighted with a marker, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You alighted the bus at that point and then you and others had to walk along that road and you walked under escort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You came walking along that road until you got to another building which you just showed us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please mark that building as well with the marker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, on Exhibit P8, if the first building may be marked as A and the second building may be marked as B. Could the witness be asked to mark, usher, as A the first building on P8 and the second building as B. You were brought, you said, to building B, which you just marked on the document P8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you were brought to that building, where were you kept inside that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we arrived in this building, we were put in the cell number 1, myself, my father, Mirsad Dizdarevic and Remsija Kutic.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall how many cells were there in total in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were 12, 11 or 12.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you describe this cell in which you were detained, the size of the cell in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the cell in which I was, cell number 1, was maybe 3 by 2, maybe even smaller. Inside the cell, there were wooden cots so to speak, I do not know if that is the right expression, like beds.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was that the place that you were expected to sleep inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How long were you detained in cell number -- in the first cell in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think up to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So that was cell number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In that hangar building, which side was cell number 1 situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to the left immediately next to the entrance to the door, so immediately to the left -- it was the first cell to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there cells constructed on either side and was there a corridor in the middle? How were the cells constructed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, along the hangar there was a hallway, and on either side there were cells along the hallway, and the entrance to the building was approximately in the middle of it, of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long was your father detained in cell number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three days, because they constantly kept bringing in Muslims, Salih Dizdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who is Salih Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is the father of Mirsad Dizdarevic. Otherwise, he was a man of religion, he was the President of the Islamic community in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: He was also brought in. How many days after you were detained was Salih Dizdarevic brought into detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was detained the next day and many other people whom I did not see immediately. However, he and -- I cannot remember the first name but last name is Krivosija, the two of them were also brought to our cell. Many other people were brought to other cells, but I could not see them, nor did I know of them immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long was your father detained in the cell, Sead Hajdarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three to four days and then since the cells were overcrowded, there were many people crammed in there, the older ones were released from the camp to go home, so it was almost some kind of house arrest, they did not have freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long were the older ones detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think three to four days, depending on who was brought in when, because every day they were bringing in more people.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know for how long Salih Dizdarevic was detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think three days, because my father was there from the first day, so that it was four days and then Salih would have been there three days.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was there any office in the building in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a small office to the right of the entrance to the building where there were the guards, the camp commander, his deputies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you see the camp commander when you were detained in cell number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many days after you were detained did you see the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on the second day, when Salih Dizdarevic was brought in, because he protested with the commander, the camp commander, so that we could see him in the hallway as Salih came out and that is when I saw him for the first time, because the cells were closed and we could not see much.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you learn who the camp commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aleksovski, the gentleman that is sitting over there to my left.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know that he was the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out from the guards whom I personally knew, and I spoke to some of them, and also the gentleman issued certain orders to the guards, so it was not difficult to conclude this.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In cell number 1, when you were detained in cell number 1, did you have any toilet facilities in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have any toilet facilities in the building in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a toilet in the building, but a makeshift one without any hygienic conditions. It was on the left-hand side of the hallway in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have free use of the toilet facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, if somebody needed to use the toilet, we had to knock on the door of the cell and if the guard who was there, if he saw it fit, he would then allow us to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long were you in cell number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think up to ten days, and then I was transferred to cell number 5 and then later to cell number 4. They were transferring us because many of the cells were overcrowded and so wherever there would be a little opening, a little space, that is where we would be put.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So you were first transferred to cell number 5, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many others were detained in cell number 5 on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to remember right now, about 15, 12 to 15, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long were you detained in cell number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I only stayed there for two days, and then I was moved to cell number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people were detained in cell number 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In cell number 4 we were ten.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you ever transferred from cell number 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I stayed there until the day when I was exchanged, when the Red Cross organised our exchange. I remained in that cell until that day.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In January when you were arrested it was the winter months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was it cold at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have cold weather during that season; that particular year there were not terrible colds.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have sufficient heating facilities in your cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: During the period of your detention, did you have facilities for religious observances in the place of detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first when Salih Dizdarevic arrived, and he has a strong personality, and he insisted with the warden to set up conditions for those who wanted to observe religious rites and after the conversation with the warden, we found out these rites could be performed in the cell, but that it should not be done aloud. However, after the release of Salih Dizdarevic from the camp, these activities were interrupted and the people who were in this camp did not have hygienic conditions in which they could perform these rites.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Why do you say they did not have hygienic conditions to perform the rites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we could not wash our hands, we could not drink water when we wanted to do it and as far as I recall, at the door to the toilet in the camp, there was a barrel filled with water and a small mug and that is how we could drink water from there, but we had no conditions to wash -- to have ablutions, because this is what needs to be done before the rite.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: At the time you were detained in the camp at Kaonik, were you taken out for deployment or work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken to dig three times to the front-lines and naturally I was escorted by armed guards, members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were taken three times to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you taken alone when you were taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were taken there as a group.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many of you were taken for trench digging on these three separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the demands of their commanders. However many people they needed, that is how many went. They would simply come to the camp, they would come into the hallway, they would call people out by their names and we would have to respond wherever we were, in whatever cell, and then the guards would take us to dig trenches on the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was the first occasion on which you were taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, because I preferred not to remember many things.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were you taken to the first time for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was taken to Presage.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you were taken to Presage, were you taken alone or were others taken with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were other people too.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On that occasion, how did they select you for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They simply had an order, they made a list and they came into the hallway and they started calling people out and you simply had to answer, and then the guard would open the door, the guard would turn you over to the person who came to get these people and they would take you up to those places and you would do whatever you were told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would bring the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly the guards read those lists out, the prison guards, they were reading them.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you came out upon hearing your name, who would take you out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we would be taken over by the HVO members, either the commanders or regular soldiers, whoever came.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So when you were taken to Presage for trench digging, that was the procedure adopted for selection for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you taken elsewhere for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken to Poodle and Kuala. This is an area of Kuala, Kuala is a more general term, it is a larger area but I am referring to the area known as Donje Kula, lower Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be permitted to show to the witness a map of the area which I intend to mark as Prosecution Exhibit 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can you please show it to the Defence first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Hajdarevic, could you please show us on the map that you have before you, Exhibit P9, Prosje where you were first taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was taken here, but it cannot be seen very well. It would be Prosje, it is somewhere round here. It is shown here as a village on this map, but we were above the village, here somewhere (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You were above the village of Prosje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I think we have been given the wrong map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you were taken to Prosje for trench digging, how long did you have to dig trenches for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until we finished a certain part of the task that was assigned to us, so we had to stay as long as it took. That time we finished it quickly, so we did not stay long, about eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please mark the area of Prosje on that map with a coloured marker? Please place a letter A on that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On the second occasion when you were taken for trench digging, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time I was taken to Podjele.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please mark Podjele on the map? Could you mark it as B, Mr. Hajdarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How long after the first trench digging, how many days after the first trench digging were you taken to Podjele for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was three or four days afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So after trench digging in Prosje you were brought back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was the procedure adopted for selection for trench digging in Podjele about three or four days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same principle, the same method was applied, everything was the same. They would simply come, call out, call you out, you had to answer and then they would take you wherever they thought it to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would call out the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would take you for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On the second occasion, for how long were you digging trenches in Podjele?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four to five hours. We did not even work there, because their commander -- Podjele before the war was inhabited by Serbs and then after Croats from Kotovaros settled there and then their commander probably wanted to act as a gentleman and he would not let us dig, he talked to us just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were also taken to Kula for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Even on that occasion, the guards would come and read out the list of names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many of you were taken to Kula for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion, about 20 of us were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you came out of your cells, the HVO would take you to Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please mark with the letter C the place Kula where you were taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kula is a wider area, the name applies to this whole area, but I will indicate the exact spot where we were put up in a house and it was in the surroundings of that house that we did the digging. Shall I put a letter C?

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mark it with C, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long did you dig trenches at Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were kept there for 36 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many of you were taken to Kula for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty or so, I cannot remember the exact number, but there was quite a large group of us, because upon our arrival here in this area, the HVO combatants first lined us up, then they robbed us. They took away our money, any valuables, gold, even some clothing, they took my shoes and my jacket. One of the soldiers said he needed it more for his operations than I did in the camp. They gave me an old pair of boots. Having robbed us there, they divided us up into two groups. One group stayed here near these houses to dig, whereas the rest of us were taken somewhere around here, right to these buildings, to dig trenches (indicates). This other group that stayed behind did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where did they dig trenches, the other group that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed near the houses that I have marked; that is the place where we were taken, whereas we were taken about 700 or 800 metres beyond those buildings, through a wood and some meadows to dig trenches for their fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many of you were in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you know any others who were in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who are they, by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Alija Beslic, then Lulo, I cannot recall his surname, then Meho Beslic, Alija Beslic, Adnan Malkic and some others whose names I cannot recall just now.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In Kula when your group was engaged in trench digging, you said you had to dig for about 36 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you dig for 36 hours continuously without a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a break of about 45 minutes, the time needed to take us from this spot to these houses. Probably they were changing shifts, so they brought us back and then they took us back during the night to do some more digging. During the digging, we were not allowed to stand upright, we had to keep working, because if you did stretch your back then the soldier who saw you would hit you either with his rifle butt or would kick you or would hit you with anything else. Before that, as soon as we had been brought there to this location where we were digging the trenches, one of their soldiers systematically mistreated and beat people to find out whether people had any valuables concealed. He beat me personally, I had two broken ribs on the right-hand side, I had to kneel before him for him to ask me questions, all kinds of questions, whether I had any gold, where I kept my money, my car, weapons and so on. If he was dissatisfied with the answer, he would kick us like a football. I know that his nickname was "Chetnik". So he would take us out systematically one by one from the trench to question us, and then he would send us back into the canal, where we had to keep on working without any rest, without food, without water and then the next day in the morning, they would humiliate us further. They brought us that morning for breakfast something, but when they emptied this package, we thought it was a meal, but when they emptied the box, we saw that they were just empty tins and they said, "here you are balijas, eat, this is your breakfast".

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of others who were beaten like you whilst you were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us were beaten. I cannot remember exactly whether anyone was spared, but one of the people who was most badly hurt was Dzafic Zehrudin, who was in this other group, and Meho Beslic. They even cracked his skull and Zehrudin Dzafic had several teeth broken. I think the Red Cross has a record of this, because the injuries were visible. Meho's head was bandaged. I think they took him to a doctor upon his return to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether any detainees were killed whilst trench digging in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see any, but after the end --

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody was killed in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The next day when the shift arrived, there were 12 people who had arrived, among whom there were two I knew and unfortunately both of them were killed, Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic. They were brought to take our place and they stayed that night and they were killed that night there. There was another killing, but again I was not an eyewitness, this was in Prosje, a man was killed, his nickname was "Cakara". I do not know his exact first name and last name, but his nickname was "Cakara".

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After the deployment in Kula, you and the others were brought back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Hajdarevic, when you were detained in the camp, do you recall any visits to the camp by members of international humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the International Red Cross visited us and they registered us as prisoners. Afterwards, I think there were two visits, on this occasion and once again when they allowed anyone who wanted to write a letter for Zenica, or something like that. We sent letters but we never got any replies.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When the ICRC visited you, you were registered as a prisoner in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am moving to tender two documents, his certificate of registration issued by the ICRC as a detainee and a copy of an identification card that was issued by the ICRC. The Defence may have a look at it and if I may be permitted to mark these exhibits as Prosecution Exhibits P10 and P11, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Before continuing, M Dubuisson, what is the number of this map that was looked at?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The one we have now on the screen, on the monitor, is exhibit number 9. It was submitted as exhibit number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Could you please show these documents to Mr. Mikulicic, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have copies of the same document for the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of P9 for the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I thought I gave a copy of P9 for the court. I am sorry if I did not tender them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to comment regarding Exhibit P9, a copy is going to be made in a minute by the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: May I tender copies of P10 and P11 to the court? There is a copy for the Defence as well. Your Honours, P10 would be the letter and P11 would be the copy of the identification card. May I proceed, your Honour? You have before you the document marked P10 which was issued by the International Committee of the Red Cross, and P11, the document marked P11 is a copy of the identification card that was also issued to you by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: According to the document P10, do you know when you were registered by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When the ICRC visited the camp -- how many times did the ICRC visit the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think apart from the time when they registered us, I think they came two more times, but I am not sure of that. Once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The day you were registered, were all the prisoners shown to the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that, because we had no insight into the number of people that were there. We just knew that apart from us in those cells, locked up in the cells, there was another hangar behind this building and that there were other people brought there. But we did not know how many, whether they had been registered or not, but I assume that all of them were not registered.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know whether attempts were made to hide prisoners from the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because on the day of the exchange, when we were to be released from the prison, some 20 men, among whom were some relatives and friends of mine, they were hidden and taken to a building that I think I already marked with the letter A, that is building number 1 at the entry to the camp, and they tried to conceal them. However, upon our insistence with the International Red Cross representatives that they too be released, representatives of the Red Cross insisted and they refused to leave the camp and complete the exchange until those people were brought over and released together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That was on the day you were released from custody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when the exchange was to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How long after the first visit of the ICRC were you released -- were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six days later, on 8th February the exchange took place and I was exchanged then.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On the day of the exchange, do you know who was present in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the warden, the commander of the camp was there then, Zlatko Aleksovski, his deputy Marko Krilic, some guards and representatives of the Red Cross, as well as their interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many detainees were exchanged on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know the exact number, but at least 100 or 150 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What time of the day were you exchanged on 8th February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That morning, I tried to go to the toilet and one of their employees, an investigator, Zeljo Katava, saw me in the corridor and when I came out of the toilet he told me to come to be interrogated. This was about 9.00. When I entered this office that they had at the entrance to the building, he asked me where I was, that they had been looking for me for five or six days, that they wanted to interrogate me, that they could not trace me and at that moment Red Cross representatives appeared, so the exchange took place at 10.00 or 11.00. As we waited for this other group of people to be released, the group that had been concealed, I think that it took a little longer, it may have been noon.

utterances.speaker: MR.. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you were exchanged, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I think it is 5.30 now, it is time for us to complete today's hearing, so we will resume work tomorrow at 10.00. Thank you very much for your testimony for today and we will see you again tomorrow. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
